explain.summary: Sam's body has two routes from eye to hands. A protective reflex is a short route that doesn't wait for the thinking part of the brain, so it is very fast. Deciding where to dive goes through the brain, so it takes longer — but practice speeds it up, and tiredness or short sleep slow it down. Whether a save is possible depends on how much time the ball gives her.
rules: Time to react = distance ÷ shot speed.
The reflex route takes about 0.10 seconds and doesn't change with practice.
Deciding takes about 0.25 seconds at first and gets about 0.003 s faster for each hour of practice, but never faster than 0.19 s.
Tiredness adds about 0.06 s and each step of short sleep adds about 0.03 s to deciding.
If the ball arrives before the deciding route finishes, only the reflex makes it in time.

source.fact: In a reflex, the signal goes along a nerve to the spinal cord and straight back out to a muscle, without involving the brain.
Simple reaction time to something you see averages about 190 milliseconds or more for college students.
Reaction time depends on things like practice and fatigue.
Not getting enough sleep can slow reaction time and cause more mistakes.

choice.what: A dive decision takes about 0.25 s, slower than a simple 0.19 s reaction
choice.why: Choosing which way to dive is harder than pressing one button when a light comes on, and harder choices take longer.

choice.what: The reflex route takes about 0.10 s
choice.why: A protective blink-and-flinch is quicker than any decision. The exact time differs between reflexes, so we used one round number.

choice.what: Practice, tiredness and sleep change the decision time by fixed amounts
choice.why: Real effects vary a lot between people; fixed steps show the direction clearly.

choice.what: Hands reach the ball as soon as a route finishes
choice.why: We left out the time it takes to actually move the arms, to keep the focus on the nerve pathways.

illustrative: Sam's shot speed (20 m/s) is a made-up value for a hard shot by a teen player.
The sizes of the practice, tiredness and sleep effects are illustrative.

citations.title: Reflex Arc: A No-Brainer
citations.supports: Shows a reflex: the signal travels along a nerve to the spinal cord, is passed to a motor nerve and sent straight back to a muscle; the whole reflex happens without involving the brain.

citations.title: Evaluation of Simple Visual Reaction Time of Different Colored Light Stimuli in Visually Normal Students (Clinical Optometry)
citations.supports: States that average simple visual reaction time for college students is about 190 ms or more, and lists practice and fatigue among the things that affect reaction time.

citations.title: Sleep Deprivation and Deficiency: How Sleep Affects Your Health
citations.publisher: NIH National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute
citations.supports: Says sleep deficiency can slow reaction time, cause more mistakes and make decisions harder.

does: Shows how little time a fast shot leaves and how it shrinks as the shot gets closer
Shows a fixed fast reflex route and a slower deciding route
Shows practice, tiredness and sleep changing only the deciding route
doesnt: Measure any real person — times are rounded teaching values
Include the time to move the arms or the ball slowing down
Say how good a goalkeeper anyone is
limits.text: This is a simplified learning model. Real people vary with age, fitness and health. The numbers are illustrative, not measurements of any real person.
limits.wellbeing: Protect your eyes and head in sport — a reflex is fast, but goggles or a helmet is faster.
